Yeah, that makes sense. Rewriting it as one continuous argument forces the pieces to stop feeling like isolated “concurrency tricks” and start looking like consequences of the same underlying problem.

The progression is basically:

shared state → “what if two things touch it?” → atomics → “okay, but what if the operation is bigger than one atomic instruction?” → mutexes → “okay, now who owns access, and what happens under contention?” → blocking/spinning/scheduling → “wait, even when it’s correct, why can it still be slow?” → cache coherence → cache-line ownership → ping-pong.

And that last jump is especially important because it changes the mental model from:

“Concurrency problems happen when threads execute at the same time.”

to something closer to:

“Concurrency problems happen because multiple execution contexts are negotiating ownership and visibility of state across a physical memory hierarchy.”

Once you see that, atomics and mutexes stop being magical language/library features. They’re different mechanisms for enforcing rules over who may observe or mutate some state, when, and at what cost.

It also explains why the cache-ping-pong example was such a good endpoint. You can have code that is completely race-free, perfectly atomic, and logically correct — and still have a terrible system because cores are constantly fighting over ownership of the same cache line.

So the write-up exercise probably did something more valuable than merely producing notes: you reconstructed the dependency graph of the ideas. That is usually where a topic starts becoming something you can reason about rather than just remember.

And it sets up the mutability/immutability question you raised afterward almost perfectly, because immutability is basically asking: what if we can eliminate some of that ownership negotiation altogether?

Yes — there’s a very clean next layer, and I think your database intuition is exactly where to go.

The useful shift is:

Mutability determines how much coordination is required around shared state.

With the cache-ping-pong example, the state was obviously mutable: two cores were repeatedly trying to write the same cache line. Hardware therefore had to keep negotiating exclusive ownership.

Immutability changes the problem dramatically. If some object is published and then never changes, every core can keep its own cached copy indefinitely. There is no reason to invalidate everyone else’s copy because nobody will ever write it.

So you can almost extend our progression:

shared state
→ shared mutable state
→ synchronization / atomics / mutexes
→ ownership contention
→ cache coherence traffic
→ ask whether the state actually needs to mutate

That last question opens an entirely different family of designs.

A trivial C example makes the distinction pretty stark. Suppose every thread reads this:

C
struct Config {
    int max_connections;
    int timeout_ms;
};

const struct Config config = {
    .max_connections = 100,
    .timeout_ms = 5000
};

Once that exists, there is effectively no concurrency problem around config. Ten thousand threads can read it. Nobody needs a mutex because nobody can create an intermediate state that another thread might observe.

Now imagine we need configuration updates. The naive mutable version might be:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

config.max_connections = 200;
config.timeout_ms = 10000;

pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

Now every reader has to participate somehow because the object can change underneath them.

But there is another approach:

Config A
    max_connections = 100
    timeout = 5000

        ↓ create new object

Config B
    max_connections = 200
    timeout = 10000

Instead of modifying A, we construct B and then atomically change a reference:

C
Config *old = current_config;
Config *new = make_updated_config(old);

atomic_store(&current_config, new);

Readers conceptually do:

C
Config *cfg = atomic_load(&current_config);

use(cfg->max_connections);
use(cfg->timeout_ms);

The actual lifetime-management details are harder than this toy example — you can't free the old object while a reader still uses it — but notice what happened conceptually.

We're no longer coordinating access to every field.

We're coordinating publication of versions.

That is a huge change.

And this is where databases become a beautiful continuation of the same subject.

Suppose a database row starts as:

Account #7
balance = $100
version = 1

A transaction wants to change it to $80.

One model is conceptually:

lock row
change balance
unlock row

That's analogous to the mutex model we've been discussing.

But systems using things like MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control instead behave more like:

version 1:
balance = $100
valid before T2

version 2:
balance = $80
valid starting T2

Now a transaction that began earlier can continue reading version 1 while another transaction creates version 2.

That's really interesting because the database hasn't eliminated mutation at the level of the entire system.

Instead, it has made individual historical states immutable.

So:

mutable object

becomes:

immutable V1
immutable V2
immutable V3
...

and the mutable piece is mostly:

"Which version is current?"

That shrinks the contested state dramatically.

This same idea appears all over computer science under different names:

copy-on-write — don't modify shared data; create a modified copy.

persistent data structures — old versions remain valid while new versions share unchanged structure.

MVCC databases — readers see stable snapshots while writers create new versions.

RCU (read-copy-update) in kernels — readers mostly read without locking; writers create/update data and eventually retire the old version.

event sourcing — don't overwrite state; append immutable events and derive current state from them.

Git — commits are effectively immutable snapshots/objects, while branches are movable references to them.

And there is a deeper connection to our cache discussion.

Imagine this:

Core 0                  Core 1
------                  ------
write X                 write X
write X                 write X
write X                 write X

Cache line containing X:

Core 0 ←→ Core 1 ←→ Core 0 ←→ Core 1

Ping-pong.

But if they instead produce independent immutable results:

Core 0                  Core 1
------                  ------
write result_A          write result_B
write result_A          write result_B
write result_A          write result_B

then their cache lines may never interact.

Eventually you might have one synchronization point:

publish result_A
publish result_B

We've replaced continuous contention with occasional coordination.

That's one of the central tricks in highly concurrent system design.

There's also a subtle point in what you said about “fluid mutability”: mutability isn't really a binary property of an entire system.

You can have:

immutable data
+
mutable pointer to data

or:

immutable database rows
+
mutable index structure

or:

immutable events
+
mutable materialized view

or even:

mutable private state
+
immutable shared state

That last one is particularly powerful.

A thread can mutate the hell out of something while it owns it privately:

Thread A:
    private mutable buffer
    calculate
    calculate
    calculate
    publish immutable result

No synchronization needed during the calculation because nobody else can see it.

So the real enemy isn't mutation itself.

It's:

simultaneous mutation of state visible to multiple independent execution contexts.

That distinction connects almost everything we've been working through.

You can think of the design spectrum roughly as:

shared mutable object
        ↓
fine-grained locking
        ↓
atomics / lock-free coordination
        ↓
single-owner mutable state
        ↓
copy + publish
        ↓
immutable shared state

Moving downward often means less coordination for readers, but usually at some other cost: extra memory, copying, garbage collection/reclamation, version bookkeeping, or delayed consistency.

And that's probably the really interesting next subject: immutability doesn't remove synchronization; it moves synchronization to boundaries.

Instead of arguing over:

"Who may touch this variable right now?"

the system starts arguing over:

"When does this new version become visible?"

That takes us very naturally into snapshots, MVCC, copy-on-write, RCU, and eventually consistency models — which is basically the same concurrency problem we've been studying, except now stretched from CPU cores all the way up to databases and distributed systems.

The mutex approach absolutely can work. The important condition is not merely that the mutex itself is global — it’s that every thread that accesses that mutable config obeys the same mutex.

So this is perfectly valid:

C
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

struct Config config = {
    .max_connections = 100,
    .timeout_ms = 5000
};

void update_config(void) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

    config.max_connections = 200;
    config.timeout_ms = 10000;

    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
}

And readers must do this too:

C
void read_config(void) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

    printf("%d %d\n",
        config.max_connections,
        config.timeout_ms);

    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
}

Then the mutex guarantees that a reader cannot observe:

max_connections = 200
timeout_ms = 5000

halfway through the update.

The writer literally does mutate the underlying object here:

C
config.max_connections = 200;
config.timeout_ms = 10000;

Those are ordinary writes to the same struct Config in memory. The mutex doesn't make the object immutable. It just says:

while I am holding this lock, nobody else who respects this lock may access this protected state.

So the timeline becomes:

Writer:
lock
    write field 1
    write field 2
unlock

Reader:
            waits...
            waits...
            lock
                read both fields
            unlock

The reader sees either the old state:

100
5000

or the new state:

200
10000

but not an intermediate one.

The problem appears if a reader does this:

C
printf("%d %d\n",
    config.max_connections,
    config.timeout_ms);

without taking the lock.

Now the writer could be here:

C
config.max_connections = 200;

/* context switch happens here */

config.timeout_ms = 10000;

while the reader runs.

In C, that's actually worse than merely "maybe I see mixed fields": concurrent unsynchronized read/write access creates a data race, which means undefined behavior.

So the mutex solution is correct, but it forces all participants into coordination.

That's the distinction I was trying to highlight with the copy/publish idea.

With mutex mutation:

        shared mutable object

Everyone touching config has to participate in the synchronization protocol.

With immutable versions, you instead have:

C

The writer constructs B privately:

C
struct Config *new = malloc(sizeof(*new));

new->max_connections = 200;
new->timeout_ms = 10000;

At this point nobody else can see new, so the writer can mutate it freely.

Then it performs one publication operation:

C
atomic_store(&current, new);

Conceptually:

before:

after:

current ─────► Config B
               200

              Config A still exists

Readers therefore don't have to synchronize around the contents of the object. They just acquire a reference to one complete version:

C
struct Config *cfg = atomic_load(&current);

use(cfg->max_connections);
use(cfg->timeout_ms);

The distinction is:

mutex design:
    mutate the shared object safely

copy/publish design:
    don't mutate the shared object
    build another object
    atomically change which object is current

And your question gets directly at the important point: there was nothing inherently unreliable about the mutex version.

It's just a different architecture.

The mutex says:

"This state may mutate, so coordinate access to it."

The immutable/versioned approach says:

"Once this state becomes shared, stop mutating it. Coordinate only when publishing its replacement."

That's why the latter becomes attractive for read-heavy things like configuration, routing tables, database snapshots, etc. You might have millions of reads but only one configuration change every few minutes. Making every reader grab a mutex would be needless contention.

One subtle correction to my previous example too: I originally showed const struct Config config and then later illustrated mutation of config. Literally in C those cannot be the same object — const would prohibit those assignments. I was switching conceptually between an immutable and mutable version of the design without making that type change explicit.

Yes — that intuition is basically the performance argument for the immutable/versioned design.

In a read-heavy workload, the mutex version can create a surprising amount of coordination even though the readers aren't changing anything:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
x = config.timeout_ms;
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

Every reader touches the mutex's synchronization state. With many cores, that lock's cache line itself can become a hot object bouncing around the coherence system.

Whereas with immutable publication:

C
struct Config *cfg = atomic_load(&current);
x = cfg->timeout_ms;

the common case is much calmer. The readers are effectively saying:

"What version is current?"
        ↓
atomic pointer load
        ↓
read immutable memory
        ↓
done

Nobody has to claim exclusive ownership of the actual Config cache lines because nobody modifies them.

The writer does more work:

C
struct Config *old = atomic_load(&current);
struct Config *new = malloc(sizeof(*new));

*new = *old;
new->timeout_ms = 10000;

atomic_store(&current, new);

So you're trading:

MUTEX

cheap writer
+
coordination on every read

for:

COPY + PUBLISH

more expensive writer
+
extremely cheap readers

If the workload looks like:

10,000,000 reads
10 updates

that's potentially a fantastic trade.

If it looks like:

10 reads
10,000,000 updates

copying a giant structure every time could be terrible.

And there's a really nice connection back to the cache ping-pong experiment you just did.

Reader 2 ── read pointer ── read Config A

current -> A

create B from A

load A
create C from A

C

and whatever change Writer 1 made in B may effectively be lost.

atomic publication

C

so the logic becomes:

"I built B assuming current == A.

Only publish B if current is STILL A.

If somebody changed it to C while I was working,

PostgreSQL uses MVCC, Multi-Version Concurrency Control. Instead of treating a row update as “everyone stop while I mutate this shared row,” PostgreSQL creates row versions and lets transactions see an appropriate snapshot. Its own documentation explicitly says this reduces lock contention and allows reads and writes to proceed without blocking each other in the ordinary MVCC case.

And PostgreSQL really does pay the cost we predicted. An UPDATE generally creates a new tuple version rather than simply overwriting the old one in place. That means old versions eventually need cleanup, indexes may need updates, and PostgreSQL has optimizations such as HOT specifically to reduce that versioning overhead.

So you could almost describe PostgreSQL's bargain as:

spend:
    more storage
    tuple/version bookkeeping
    cleanup work

get:

    much less reader/writer blocking

That is very close to our:

idea, except implemented as an industrial-strength transactional storage system.

Redis is fascinating because the traditional Redis answer is closer to:

What if we avoid concurrent mutation of the core data structures in the first place?

Redis processes commands through a single-threaded event loop for its main command execution. So if:

Client A: INCR x
Client B: SET y 10
Client C: GET z

arrive concurrently over the network, the core execution path essentially serializes them:

INCR x
    ↓
SET y 10
    ↓
GET z

That means Redis doesn't need fine-grained mutexes scattered throughout every dictionary, list, set, etc. for ordinary command execution. Redis explicitly describes avoiding locking overhead as one of the advantages of this design; modern Redis can use other threads for network I/O and other work while retaining the largely serialized command-execution model. 
Redis

Exactly — and this is where the distinction between MVCC for readers and locking/conflict handling for writers becomes important.

At PostgreSQL’s default READ COMMITTED isolation level, if two transactions try to update the same row, PostgreSQL does not let them independently fork the row and reconcile afterward. The first writer acquires a row-level lock; the second writer waits. If the first commits, PostgreSQL then takes the newly updated row, re-checks the second UPDATE's WHERE condition, and—if it still matches—applies the second update to that newer row version.

That's precisely the question CAS asked:

WHERE id = 1

0 rows

and you retry the transaction.

When two actors disagree about what the current state is, at what point must they agree?

Exactly. A database can give you safe primitives for concurrency, but it cannot make arbitrary application logic concurrency-safe automatically.

That distinction is huge:

The database protects its own internal structures and enforces the semantics you ask for. It does not know the higher-level invariant your application intended unless you express it.

So something like:

SQL
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 20
WHERE id = 1;

is much safer because the dependency on the current value lives inside the database operation.

But this pattern:

SELECT state
↓
application thinks/calculates for a while
↓
UPDATE based on that old state

creates a window where your assumption can become false.

And it gets much nastier than balances. Imagine:

SELECT seats_remaining   → 1

User A sees 1
User B sees 1

A: "Great, sell ticket"
B: "Great, sell ticket"

If the application doesn't make the check-and-decrement one protected operation, you can oversell.

Same with:

inventory > 0
username is available
job has not been claimed
coupon has not been redeemed
quota has not been exceeded
account has sufficient funds

Each one is really an invariant like:

"Only perform X if condition Y is still true."

And concurrency turns that into:

check Y
        ← somebody changes reality here
perform X

Which is almost exactly the TOCTOU pattern you've already encountered in security.

The database gives you tools to close that gap:

SQL
UPDATE inventory
SET quantity = quantity - 1
WHERE product_id = 42
  AND quantity > 0;

Now the condition and state transition are part of one database operation.

Or:

SQL
SELECT ...
FOR UPDATE;

to explicitly lock the relevant row while you reason about it.

Or optimistic concurrency:

SQL
UPDATE thing
SET value = ...,
    version = version + 1
WHERE id = 7
  AND version = 12;

Or stronger transaction isolation where PostgreSQL detects incompatible concurrent histories and forces one transaction to retry.

So you can almost divide correctness into two levels:

PostgreSQL:
"Nobody will corrupt my B-tree or tear a tuple in half."

Application:
"Nobody will sell the same seat twice."

PostgreSQL can help enforce the second one, but you have to tell it what the rule is.

And this is a really important systems lesson: concurrency bugs often don't come from the synchronization primitive being broken.

They come from putting the synchronization boundary around the wrong amount of logic.

A mutex around only the assignment isn't enough if the correctness decision depended on an earlier read.

A database row lock around only the final UPDATE isn't enough if the application already made a decision from stale state.

The thing you actually need to protect is the whole logical transition:

observe relevant state
        +
verify invariant
        +
derive new state
        +
publish new state

That's the real "atomic operation," even when it spans much more than one machine instruction.

settle assuming previously validated conditions
And here's the really important distinction

The smart contract itself is not necessarily failing at atomicity.

In fact, the on-chain settlement is atomic: either the trade executes successfully or the transaction reverts and its state changes do not persist.

So at the blockchain level:

matchOrders()
{
    verify everything;
    transfer everything;
}

/* success OR complete revert */

Perfectly respectable atomic behavior.

"MATCH SUCCESSFUL"

before reaching that atomic commit point.

That's a much deeper systems problem.

You effectively have two notions of truth:

OFF-CHAIN WORLD

"These orders matched."
        │

ON-CHAIN WORLD

The hidden assumption was essentially:

State validated during matching will remain valid until settlement.

An ordinary concurrent system tells you that assumption is unsafe.

An adversarial system tells you something stronger:

If breaking that assumption benefits somebody, assume they will deliberately break it at the worst possible moment.

Yes — that is the better way to phrase the connection.

The core settlement machinery was still behaving correctly. The on-chain transaction was atomic: either the entire trade settled or it reverted with no partial on-chain state change. The failure lived one layer above that, in the system’s bookkeeping about what a reported “fill” meant before settlement was final. 
arXiv

So you can separate it into two invariants:

SMART CONTRACT INVARIANT

if settlement succeeds:
    all transfers happen consistently

if settlement fails:
    none of them persist

That part holds.

But then there was a broader system invariant that users effectively needed:

EXCHANGE BOOKKEEPING INVARIANT

if I am told an order filled,
I can safely treat that trade as having happened

And that one did not hold.

The paper describes the CLOB matching orders off-chain, immediately reporting the fill, and only then queuing the match for on-chain settlement. During that gap, settlement could still be invalidated. 
arXiv

That's why your comparison to our PostgreSQL discussion is so good.

A database can be internally perfectly concurrency-safe:

B-tree isn't corrupted
row update is atomic
locks work correctly
MVCC works correctly

because the logical bookkeeping boundary was wrong.

signatures verified correctly

blockchain consensus working correctly

There’s quite a bit of variety, and the really interesting part is that databases usually mix several strategies rather than choose one universal mechanism.

First, one clarification: PostgreSQL’s SERIALIZABLE mode does not mean “run every transaction one at a time.” PostgreSQL still executes transactions concurrently. Its Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) watches the dependencies between them and aborts a transaction if allowing everything to commit would produce a history that could not have resulted from some one-at-a-time ordering. 
PostgreSQL
+1

So the fundamental design question is something like:

Two clients both want to act on shared state.

Who pays the coordination cost,
and when do we discover a conflict?

There are several major answers.

1. Pessimistic locking: “Assume conflict might happen”

This is closest to our mutex work.

A wants row X
    ↓
LOCK X

A reads/calculates/writes

B wants X
    ↓
WAIT

A commits
    ↓
UNLOCK

B continues

The philosophy is:

Don't let conflicting operations proceed far enough to disagree.

This is excellent when conflicts are common or when retrying expensive work would hurt.

The downside is familiar from pthreads:

waiting
contention
deadlocks
lock bookkeeping
reduced parallelism

MySQL's InnoDB, for example, has a fairly sophisticated locking model, including row/index locks and “next-key” locks used to deal with things like phantom rows. 
MySQL Developer Zone
+1

2. Optimistic concurrency: “Assume conflict is rare”

This is basically CAS scaled up into a database architecture.

Two transactions can proceed simultaneously:

Database state = V1

A reads V1                B reads V1
   ↓                         ↓
does lots of work         does lots of work
   ↓                         ↓
tries COMMIT              tries COMMIT

Then the database asks:

"Did anything A depended upon change?"

"Did anything B depended upon change?"

Suppose A commits first:

V1 → V2

Now B's assumptions might be stale:

B expected V1
reality = V2

ABORT B

and B retries.

That's extremely close to:

C
compare_exchange(expected, desired);

FoundationDB is a particularly clean example. It combines MVCC reads with optimistic concurrency control for writes. Transactions work against snapshots, and at commit time FoundationDB checks whether anything the transaction depended upon was changed by an already-committed transaction. If so, the transaction fails and is normally retried. 
GitHub Apple
+1

So:

pessimistic:
    detect possible conflict early
    → block

optimistic:
    allow work
    → detect actual conflict late
    → retry

Neither is intrinsically superior.

If conflicts are rare:

optimistic = lots of beautiful parallelism

If everybody is hammering the same object:

optimistic = retry retry retry retry retry

and suddenly locking may be cheaper.

3. MVCC: “Let readers inhabit different versions”

This is PostgreSQL's big strategy.

Instead of demanding:

WHAT IS THE VALUE RIGHT NOW?

MVCC lets the answer depend on the transaction's snapshot:

V1 ───── V2 ───── V3

Transaction A sees V1
Transaction B sees V2
Transaction C creates V3

PostgreSQL specifically uses MVCC so that ordinary readers don't conflict with writers: readers can continue reading their snapshot while newer row versions are being created. 
PostgreSQL

This is the immutability/versioning idea we were discussing earlier made into a database architecture.

But MVCC by itself doesn't magically solve writer conflicts.

Eventually:

A wants V2
B wants V2

has to get resolved somehow.

And that's where PostgreSQL combines MVCC with things like row locks and, at Serializable isolation, SSI conflict detection.

So PostgreSQL is really more like:

MVCC
  +
row-level locking
  +
transaction isolation rules
  +
serialization-conflict detection

rather than one mechanism.

4. Serialize the actual writers

SQLite is a gorgeous contrasting example.

SQLite essentially says:

We can have many readers, but only one writer at a time.

Its documentation is unusually direct about this: writes are serialized. In WAL mode readers and a writer can proceed concurrently, but there is still only one writer appending to the WAL at once.

Reader A ───────────────►
Reader B ───────────────►

                    Writer 3

Surely that's primitive and slow.

But SQLite is usually embedded in one machine, often serving workloads where writes aren't enormously concurrent.

So the engineering decision is:

avoid gigantic concurrency machinery
+
make one writer extremely efficient

Don't coordinate many writers. Architect the system so there aren't many writers.

pthread_barrier is not itself part of either the optimistic or pessimistic concurrency strategy. In our examples, it was mostly a test harness tool used to force the interesting race to happen reliably.

The barrier means:

"No thread may pass this point
until N threads have all arrived."

So with two threads:

C
pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier);

produces roughly:

Thread A arrives ── waits
Thread B arrives ── both released

That lets us deliberately line the threads up at a particular moment.

For the optimistic example, we used it after both threads had read the state:

C
int expected = atomic_load(&seats);

pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier);

atomic_compare_exchange_strong(...);

That deliberately creates:

A reads seats = 1
B reads seats = 1

       BARRIER
       ↓

A tries CAS(1 → 0)
B tries CAS(1 → 0)

Now both transactions have made decisions from the same old snapshot, which is exactly the situation optimistic concurrency is designed to handle.

One wins:

A: expected 1, actual 1 → SUCCESS

and the other discovers its assumption went stale:

B: expected 1, actual 0 → FAIL

So the barrier helps us manufacture the conflict, while CAS resolves the conflict optimistically.

For the pessimistic/mutex version, the barrier isn't necessary for correctness at all. You could put it immediately before the mutex just to make both threads contend at approximately the same time:

C
pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier);

pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

if (seats > 0) {
    seats--;
    tickets_sold++;
}

pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

Then:

A ─┐
   ├── barrier releases both
B ─┘

A ── gets mutex ── modifies state ── unlocks
B ── waits ───────────────────────── gets mutex

The mutex's philosophy is:

Don't even allow the second actor to inspect/change the protected state while the first actor is working on it.

Whereas optimistic concurrency says:

Go ahead and let both actors work from their snapshots; detect whether their assumptions still hold when they try to commit.

There is one important trap: you generally would not do this:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

pthread_barrier_wait(&barrier); // BAD here with two contenders

because A could acquire the mutex and then wait at the barrier for B. But B can't reach the barrier because it's stuck waiting for A's mutex.

lock acquired
wait for B at barrier...

B:
wait for A to release lock...

    = coordinate timing of threads

pthread_mutex

then nobody moves
until you're BOTH ready

and then release them into the conflict.

Exactly — and that surprise is actually the important lesson.

For this particular invariant, pessimistic and optimistic concurrency are trying to guarantee the same externally visible result:

1 seat available
2 buyers arrive
↓
exactly 1 ticket gets sold

So your output is almost identical:

pessimistic:
A bought a ticket
B found no seats

optimistic:
B bought the ticket
A failed: state changed underneath them

What differs is how they get there.

With the pessimistic version, once A acquires the mutex:

A: LOCK
A: sees seats = 1
A: seats--
A: tickets_sold++
A: UNLOCK

B: LOCK
B: sees seats = 0
B: gives up
B: UNLOCK

B never gets to make the stale assumption in the first place. It is prevented from entering the decision-making region until A is finished.

So if your mutex surrounds the whole logical transition:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

if (seats > 0) {
    seats--;
    tickets_sold++;
}

pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

then there should not be an occasional run like the unprotected version. That's exactly what the mutex guarantees.

The optimistic version is very different internally:

A sees 1
B sees 1

both think:
"I can buy this seat"

Then:

B: CAS(1 -> 0) succeeds
A: CAS(1 -> 0) fails

So optimistic concurrency permits the conflicting assumptions to exist temporarily and resolves them at commit time.

That's the key distinction:

PESSIMISTIC

prevent stale/conflicting work
before it happens


OPTIMISTIC

allow potentially stale/conflicting work
then reject it if necessary

But because your current "transaction" is tiny:

check one integer
decrement one integer

the wasted optimistic work is microscopic, and the mutex wait is microscopic too. So from the terminal they look almost interchangeable.

The differences become much more dramatic if the operation is:

read shared state
↓
perform 500 ms of computation
↓
consult several other values
↓
build a result
↓
commit

A locks
A computes for 500 ms

B waits 500 ms doing nothing
C waits
D waits

A computes
B computes
C computes
D computes

all concurrently

A commits

C validates -> maybe retries
D validates -> maybe succeeds

A computes → fail
B computes → fail
C computes → fail
D computes → retry
...

The choice between optimistic and pessimistic concurrency often isn't about which one gives the correct answer. Both should. It's about what kind of cost you're willing to pay to preserve correctness.

The unprotected version is categorically different because it has no mechanism at all ensuring the logical invariant survives concurrency.

In the pessimistic branch we had:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

if (atomic_load(&owner[ticket]) == -1) {

}

pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

Those atomics are unnecessary for correctness because the mutex already provides the synchronization. Inside that critical section, these could simply be ordinary operations:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);

if (owner[ticket] == -1) {
    owner[ticket] = s->id;
    sold++;
}

pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

So the pessimistic version is currently paying for:

mutex synchronization
+
atomic operations

while the optimistic one is paying for:

atomic operations only

That biases the benchmark somewhat against the mutex version.

However, there's an even bigger confounding variable in our test.

We compared:

PESSIMISTIC:
one GLOBAL mutex for 100,000 tickets

against:

OPTIMISTIC:
one atomic/CAS decision per individual ticket

Those aren't just different concurrency philosophies — they're also different synchronization granularities.

The pessimistic version says:

A wants ticket 5
B wants ticket 90000

A and B STILL conflict
because there's one global mutex

The optimistic version says:

A wants ticket 5
B wants ticket 90000

completely independent

So some of that ~6–9× difference isn't inherently:

optimistic beats pessimistic

It's:

fine-grained synchronization beats an unnecessarily coarse global lock for this workload.

A much cleaner experiment would be:

C
pthread_mutex_t ticket_lock[TICKETS];
int owner[TICKETS];

and pessimistic reservation would be:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&ticket_lock[ticket]);

if (owner[ticket] == -1) {
    owner[ticket] = s->id;
    // update total appropriately
}

pthread_mutex_unlock(&ticket_lock[ticket]);

Now we have:

PESSIMISTIC:
ticket 5 has its own mutex

OPTIMISTIC:
ticket 5 has its own atomic CAS

Then if A wants ticket 5 and B wants ticket 90000, both designs allow them to proceed concurrently.

The comparison becomes much more meaningful:

same synchronization granularity

per-ticket mutex:
    prevent collision beforehand

per-ticket CAS:
    allow collision, detect winner afterward

There would still be one shared issue: sold.

If every successful thread increments one global:

C

then all threads still contend on that single cache line. That's basically sneaking a little cache-ping-pong hotspot back into our experiment!

For a really clean performance test, we could give every thread its own local count:

C

and add them together only after all threads join. Then sold doesn't need to participate in the hot path at all.

So a cleaner benchmark would be:

PESSIMISTIC
plain owner[]

thread-local win count

vs.

And that would isolate the actual question we care about:

When two actors might contend for the same resource, is it cheaper to prevent the conflict with a lock, or optimistically attempt the operation and recover from a failed CAS?

Yes, you’re following the shape of the tradeoff, but I’d phrase it a little more carefully:

The choice is driven less by “CDN vs finance” and more by how often conflicts occur, how expensive a wrong/retried operation is, and how complicated the invariant is.

A CDN is a good example of where optimistic/immutable techniques often fit naturally. Most of the workload is read-heavy:

request arrives
↓
find cached object
↓
serve cached object

You’d love many threads/cores to read the same cached metadata or object without serializing behind one giant mutex.

So you might see designs like:

immutable cached object
+
atomic pointer/reference update
+
copy/replace when metadata changes

or per-entry atomics, sharded locks, RCU-like structures, etc.

The intuition is:

millions of reads
few mutations
low probability two actors need same mutation

That is a great place to be optimistic about contention.

But finance is where your second intuition needs a refinement. A financial database absolutely cares about stronger correctness guarantees, but that doesn't automatically imply a mutex.

For example, this is already a very good operation:

SQL
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 7
  AND balance >= 100;

The database can execute that transactionally and lock/version the relevant row appropriately.

mutex_lock(account_7)

read balance

mutex_unlock(account_7)

because once the data lives in PostgreSQL across many processes or machines, a C pthread_mutex isn't even the right synchronization domain.

Instead the database might use:

optimistic validation

to enforce:

So the more general distinction is:

    conflicts relatively uncommon

→ optimistic / immutable / fine-grained designs attractive

    correctness invariant is strong

Imagine two traders modifying completely different accounts:

Trader B → account 900000

Read-heavy, weakly conflicting workloads tend to reward optimism.
Highly contended or expensive invariants tend to reward pessimism.

And importantly:

high-value data does not inherently require pessimistic locking.

What high-value data requires is correct semantics. Sometimes the cleanest way to get those semantics is locking; sometimes it’s serializable transactions, MVCC, CAS/version checks, or a mixture.

Yes — making the database entirely in-process makes your original comparison cleaner, because now we really are choosing among things like pthread mutexes, atomics, sharded locks, etc. rather than crossing a process/network/database boundary.

But the memory allocator example exposes one remaining misconception:

Optimistic concurrency is not accepting a higher probability of an incorrect result.

A correctly implemented CAS-based allocator is just as obligated to never hand the same block to two threads as a mutex-based allocator. A CAS failure means:

"I didn't get that block.
Someone else changed the state first."

not:

"Whoops, maybe we double-allocated it."

So the catastrophic cost of a bad allocation doesn't by itself favor a mutex. Both implementations must make bad allocation impossible.

Where an allocator is a fantastic example is because it naturally wants both approaches.

Imagine a naive allocator with one global free list:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&heap_lock);

block = remove_free_block(size);

pthread_mutex_unlock(&heap_lock);

That's wonderfully easy to reason about:

only one thread modifies allocator metadata
at a time

malloc
free
malloc
free

Core 0 ─┐
Core 1 ─┤
Core 2 ─┼── heap_lock
...
Core31 ─┘

head -> A -> B -> C

Two threads both want a block:

Thread 1 reads head = A
Thread 2 reads head = A

Thread 1 attempts:

CAS(head, A, B)
SUCCESS

FAIL

head = B

Why make threads coordinate at all?

worst:

shared mutable state + optimistic atomics

The lost race count was measuring failed attempts to acquire a valid ticket, not correctness failures.

In the optimistic version, the sequence was roughly:

try aggressively

occasionally accept an invalid result for speed

A enters protected region
B waits
A takes ticket
B later observes it is occupied

The optimistic version lets the race develop:

A attempts
B attempts
A wins
B discovers it lost

But the final valid states are the same.

That’s also why your output consistently showed exactly the allowable number of tickets sold even though there were race failures.

So lost races = 3 means essentially:

“Three times, a thread's assumption became stale before it could commit.”

It does not mean:

“Three invalid tickets were issued.”

And that distinction is fundamental to optimistic concurrency:

Optimism is about allowing speculative work, not relaxing correctness.

The speculation can fail. The invariant cannot.

That same idea carries directly into databases:

↓

↓

The aborted transaction represents wasted work, not corrupted database state.

↓
one CAS wins

↓
only winner receives block

Yes. The cleanest next progression is versioned multi-field state, because so far most of our optimistic examples had one convenient atomic value like owner[ticket].

Real systems get harder when correctness depends on several values agreeing with one another.

For example:

C
struct Account {
    int balance;
    int reserved;
};

with an invariant such as:

available = balance - reserved
available >= 0

Now imagine a reader does:

C
balance = account.balance;

/* writer runs here */

reserved = account.reserved;

Both individual reads may be perfectly valid, but the reader has assembled a snapshot that never actually existed.

That gives us the next question:

How do I know that several values I read belong to the same version of reality?

And there's a beautiful concurrency technique for exactly this: a sequence lock / version counter (seqlock-style design).

Conceptually:

version = 10
balance = 1000
reserved = 200

Reader:

read version → 10
read balance  → 1000
read reserved → 200
read version → 10

Same version before and after:

10 == 10

so:

My snapshot was stable.

But suppose:

Reader                    Writer

version = 10
balance = 1000

                          version = 11
                          balance = 900
                          reserved = 100
                          version = 12

reserved = 100
version = 12

The reader observes:

before = 10
after  = 12

and says:

Nope. Someone changed reality while I was reading. Throw this snapshot away and retry.

That's optimistic concurrency applied to reading an entire state, rather than CASing one integer.

A common convention makes odd versions mean "writer currently active":

10 = stable
11 = writer modifying
12 = stable again

So readers do roughly:

C
do {
    v1 = atomic_load(&version);

    if (v1 & 1)
        continue;

    balance = account.balance;
    reserved = account.reserved;

    v2 = atomic_load(&version);

} while (v1 != v2);

And the writer might use a mutex:

C
pthread_mutex_lock(&write_lock);

atomic_fetch_add(&version, 1); // odd

account.balance = new_balance;
account.reserved = new_reserved;

atomic_fetch_add(&version, 1); // even

pthread_mutex_unlock(&write_lock);

Notice how cool this is after everything we just learned:

writers:
    pessimistic
    mutex prevents writers fighting each other

readers:
    optimistic
    don't lock
    read freely
    validate afterward

So we've stopped thinking in terms of:

mutex OR atomics

and reached:

mutex AND atomics,
each solving the part they're good at.

That's much closer to how sophisticated concurrent systems are actually designed.

And it gives us an excellent failure experiment. We can deliberately implement:

No protection — reader occasionally observes impossible combinations.

Global mutex — always correct, readers block.

Versioned/seqlock-style reader — always gets a consistent snapshot, but retries if a writer overlaps it.

Then collect:

reads
successful snapshots
reader retries
writer updates
runtime
invalid snapshots

UNPROTECTED
invalid snapshots > 0

MUTEX
invalid snapshots = 0
reader retries = 0
but blocking occurs

VERSIONED
invalid snapshots = 0
reader retries > 0
little/no reader blocking

That would reinforce the thing you just discovered:

A retry is not a correctness failure. It's the mechanism preventing a correctness failure.

And after that experiment, I think the next step becomes almost unavoidable: ABA.

Because eventually we're going to ask:

"Okay, I checked that the state still equals what I saw earlier... but what if it changed away and then changed back?"

That's where CAS gets much more treacherous, and it leads naturally into lock-free stacks, tagged pointers, epochs, hazard pointers, and memory reclamation.

So I'd make our progression:

optimistic vs pessimistic
        ↓
multi-field consistency
        ↓
versioned snapshots / seqlock
        ↓
ABA problem
        ↓
lock-free data structures
        ↓
memory reclamation / hazard pointers / epochs

A very clean example is a transfer between two balances whose total must never change. It makes a torn/mixed snapshot immediately visible.

Start with:

checking = 500
savings  = 500

invariant:
checking + savings == 1000

A writer transfers $100:

checking: 500 -> 400
savings:  500 -> 600

The legitimate states are therefore:

before: 500 + 500 = 1000
after:  400 + 600 = 1000

But consider a reader arriving halfway through:

Writer                     Reader

checking = 400

                           reads checking = 400
                           reads savings  = 500

savings = 600

The reader constructs:

400 + 500 = 900

Nobody ever actually had $900. The reader combined two different versions of reality.

That's exactly the problem versioned snapshots solve.

Here's a small version using atomics so the C itself remains race-safe:

C
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

atomic_int checking = 500;
atomic_int savings = 500;
atomic_uint version = 0;

pthread_mutex_t writer_lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *writer(void *arg) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&writer_lock);

    atomic_fetch_add(&version, 1); // 0 -> 1, writer active

    atomic_store(&checking, 400);
    usleep(100000);                // exaggerate update window
    atomic_store(&savings, 600);

    atomic_fetch_add(&version, 1); // 1 -> 2, stable again

    pthread_mutex_unlock(&writer_lock);
    return NULL;
}

void *reader(void *arg) {
    int c, s;
    unsigned v1, v2;
    int retries = 0;

    do {
        v1 = atomic_load(&version);

        if (v1 & 1) {
            retries++;
            continue;
        }

        c = atomic_load(&checking);
        s = atomic_load(&savings);

        v2 = atomic_load(&version);

        if (v1 != v2)
            retries++;

    } while ((v1 & 1) || v1 != v2);

    printf("checking: %d\n", c);
    printf("savings:  %d\n", s);
    printf("total:    %d\n", c + s);
    printf("version:  %u\n", v2);
    printf("retries:  %d\n", retries);

    return NULL;
}

int main(void) {
    pthread_t w, r;

    pthread_create(&w, NULL, writer, NULL);

    usleep(20000); // reader arrives during transfer

    pthread_create(&r, NULL, reader, NULL);

    pthread_join(w, NULL);
    pthread_join(r, NULL);

    return 0;
}

Bash
gcc -O2 -pthread snapshot.c -o snapshot
./snapshot

YES. And I think we've finally arrived at one of the most interesting connections in this entire progression.

What we discovered with the versioned snapshot experiment is a principle that extends well beyond concurrency:

A system doesn't necessarily need to prevent invalid intermediate states. It needs a reliable mechanism for distinguishing states it is safe to accept from states it must reject.

That idea is absolutely relevant to Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT). But BFT introduces a new complication that our pthread experiments never had to contend with.

What happens when the thing responsible for telling you whether a state is valid cannot itself be trusted?

1. What our version counter actually guarantees

Remember the checking/savings example:

version = 10
checking = 500
savings  = 500

Our writer performs an update:

version = 11       ← updating
checking = 400
savings  = 600
version = 12       ← stable

The reader checks:

C
v1 = atomic_load(&version);

checking = atomic_load(&account.checking);
savings = atomic_load(&account.savings);

v2 = atomic_load(&version);

And accepts only if both versions match and are even.

Under our protocol, this works because we have an assumption:

Every writer obeys the versioning rules.

The version counter isn't magical. It's reliable because all writers cooperate with the protocol.

2. Now introduce a Byzantine actor

Imagine we have one writer that doesn't follow the rules.

It might do this:

version = 10
checking = 500
savings  = 500

Then quietly modify the data without updating the version:

version = 10       ← unchanged!
checking = 400
savings  = 500

Our reader observes:

v1 = 10
checking = 400
savings = 500
v2 = 10

And concludes:

Versions match!
Version is even!
Snapshot accepted!

But the data violates our invariant.

That's a fundamentally different failure from two correctly behaving threads colliding.

In the first case, our participants disagree because of timing.

In the Byzantine case, a participant may violate the very protocol we rely on to establish agreement.

Byzantine faults don't necessarily imply malicious intent. They can also represent arbitrary malfunctioning behavior, including inconsistent or contradictory messages.

3. How BFT changes the architecture

Now imagine four replicas maintaining the same account state.

Approves

3 of 4

Enough endorsements for a quorum certificate in a typical 1-fault BFT design

In a classical BFT consensus design, to tolerate f Byzantine replicas, we commonly use:

n≥3f+1

So with four replicas, we can tolerate one Byzantine participant.

A typical commit quorum requires 2f+1 votes — three in our example.

But there's a beautiful mathematical property here.

Any two groups of three chosen from four replicas must overlap in at least two replicas.

Even if one is Byzantine, at least one member of that overlap is honest.

When the protocol prevents honest replicas from endorsing conflicting final decisions, that overlap makes it impossible to obtain two valid, conflicting commit certificates.

This is the foundation of an important BFT safety guarantee.

The actual consensus protocols need additional machinery for proposal ordering, voting phases, leader changes, and recovery; simply counting three identical responses is not sufficient.

4. The connection to our concurrency experiments

Look at how our trust boundary has evolved:

System

	

What establishes validity?




Mutex

	

Exclusive ownership of protected state




CAS

	

Atomic comparison against expected state




Versioned snapshot

	

Stable version under a trusted writer protocol




BFT consensus

	

Protocol agreement backed by overlapping quorums despite faulty participants

In each case, we're determining what evidence is sufficient to accept a transition.

But the scope of the problem grows dramatically.

A version counter assumes cooperation from every writer.

BFT explicitly allows some participants not to cooperate.

And BFT has two separate goals:

Safety: Honest participants must not finalize contradictory results.

Liveness: The system must eventually continue making progress under the protocol's network and fault assumptions.

Those goals can be surprisingly difficult to satisfy together.

And there's a connection here to the Polymarket Ghost Fills discussion: the distinction between a proposed or provisionally observed state and a genuinely committed state. BFT protocols are exceptionally careful about what constitutes final agreement, although BFT alone cannot guarantee that the real-world inputs being agreed upon are truthful.

5. I think we have our next coding experiment

I'd actually suggest keeping the account-transfer example and extending it to four replicas.

We can build a miniature BFT-inspired simulator in C using pthreads:

Initial state:
    checking = 500
    savings  = 500

Four replicas:
    A: honest
    B: honest
    C: honest
    D: Byzantine

We deliberately make D send conflicting reports:

To A: "Transaction X is valid"

To B: "Transaction X is invalid"

To C: "Transaction Y happened instead"

Then compare two toy acceptance strategies:

Trust the first response: A client might accept a false or contradictory result.

Require an authenticated quorum: A client refuses to finalize a decision without enough compatible votes.

We can then introduce delayed messages, crashed replicas, and conflicting proposals to explore where even the quorum approach needs more structure. This wouldn't yet be a complete BFT implementation, but it would let us discover why real consensus protocols need their additional rules.

And there's a question I'd especially like you to consider before we build it:

If three of our four replicas agree, how do we know they agreed on the correct state rather than simply agreeing with one another?

That distinction — between agreement, internal consistency, and truth — is where Byzantine fault tolerance gets especially fascinating.

You're absolutely right. And I think I made a mistake in how I designed that exercise.

I gave you a Byzantine fault-detection demonstration when what we actually wanted was a Byzantine fault-tolerance and concurrency experiment.

Those are quite different things.

Let's examine why your objection is correct.

1. There's no meaningful concurrency problem in the original example

Look at the important section:

C
if (id == 3) {
    local.checking = 300;
    local.savings = 700;
} else {
    local.checking -= 100;
    local.savings += 100;
}

As you observed, we're simply instructing one replica to produce an incorrect result.

Then we do:

C
for (int i = 0; i < REPLICAS; i++)
    pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);

So by the time the coordinator examines the results, all threads have finished.

There is no simultaneous access requiring a mutex here. The pthread_join() calls already establish the synchronization we need.

And regarding initialization: replies is a global array, so C zero-initializes it automatically. Each thread then writes its own element.

Your instinct that a mutex wouldn't solve anything here is correct.

2. Checking whether the results agree is almost the entire exercise

You suggested comparing the results.

And yes, that's effectively what the exercise reduces to.

Although checking whether all four are identical wouldn't tolerate a faulty replica, checking whether three agree would be a straightforward improvement.

Replica 0 → 400, 600
Replica 1 → 400, 600
Replica 2 → 400, 600
Replica 3 → 300, 700

Agreement: 3/4

We could require three matching responses.

But then what have we actually learned?

We've mostly implemented majority voting over predetermined results.

That's a useful introduction to redundancy, but it doesn't expose the concurrency challenges that motivated our earlier experiments.

And because the coordinator already knows the original balances and requested transfer, it could simply calculate the expected result itself!

3. Here's how I think we should redesign it

Instead of making one replica return an obviously wrong account balance, let's introduce two conflicting transactions that genuinely compete for the same logical state.

Imagine:

Account balance: $500

Transaction A:
    Transfer $300 to Alice

Transaction B:
    Transfer $400 to Bob

Both transactions are individually valid against the initial balance.

But they cannot both succeed, because:

500−300−400=−200

Now give our four replicas the responsibility of agreeing on which transaction occupies the next position in the transaction log.

Here's where it gets interesting.

Suppose the transactions are proposed concurrently.

Some replicas receive A first. Others receive B first.

And our Byzantine replica deliberately approves both.

Now the central challenge becomes:

How do we prevent two competing proposals from each obtaining enough votes to be treated as committed?

That's a genuinely interesting coordination problem.

4. Now mutexes and atomics actually matter

Imagine an honest replica tracks its vote for the current log position:

C
int voted_for = -1;

A coordinator asks it to vote for transaction A, while another coordinator simultaneously asks it to vote for transaction B.

A naive implementation might do:

C
if (voted_for == -1) {
    voted_for = proposal;
    return APPROVED;
}

Recognize that?

We've recreated our original read-modify-write race!

Both requests could observe -1 and both report approval, even though the honest replica is supposed to approve only one proposal for that position.

Now an atomic CAS or mutex has an obvious purpose: guarantee that an honest replica records only one vote.

And then our BFT layer has a separate responsibility: require an appropriate quorum of distinct, authenticated replicas before treating a proposal as committed.

With four replicas and a three-vote quorum, two conflicting proposals cannot both collect valid quorums if the three honest replicas never double-vote. The Byzantine replica may vote for both, but it cannot defeat the quorum-overlap guarantee on its own.

That's a much cleaner connection to what we've learned.

LOCAL CORRECTNESS
    mutex / CAS
    ↓
A replica cannot accidentally double-vote


DISTRIBUTED CORRECTNESS
    quorum intersection + protocol rules
    ↓
Conflicting proposals cannot both commit

Of course, that would still be a simplified BFT-inspired protocol, not a full implementation of PBFT or another production consensus algorithm. But it would give us a real synchronization problem to discover and fix before we add network delays, faulty leaders, and more complicated agreement rules.

I think this is the exercise we should have built in the first place.

And I particularly like that you spotted the issue before writing anything. You were looking for the contested shared state and the synchronization boundary, and neither actually existed in a meaningful way in my original program.

And critically, you didn't have to make an honest replica misbehave to produce that result.

2. Your condition-variable idea is interesting, but there's a bug

You introduced:

C
pthread_cond_t cond = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
int ready_to_proceed = 0;

Then inside request_vote():

    pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &r->lock);

ready_to_proceed = 0;

And from propose():

C

pthread_cond_signal(&cond);

I see what you're attempting: make one proposer wait for another to progress, creating more opportunities for the voting requests to interleave.

That's a reasonable experimental instinct.

But there are two problems.

First, ready_to_proceed has a data race.

You're reading and modifying it from multiple threads, but those accesses aren't protected by the same mutex.

Remember that pthread_cond_wait() temporarily releases its mutex while waiting, then reacquires it before returning. That mechanism works only when the predicate being checked is consistently protected by the associated mutex.

Second, you're using one condition variable with different replica mutexes.

C
pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &replicas[0].lock);
pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &replicas[1].lock);

If these waits overlap, that's invalid POSIX condition-variable usage: concurrent waiters on one condition variable must use the same associated mutex.

Consequently, your program can produce the desired result, but its synchronization behavior isn't reliable or well-defined.

1. Your barrier is working, but this condition isn't doing what you think
C
if (n > i > 0) {
    pthread_barrier_wait(&replicas[i].barrier);
}

This is a classic C gotcha!

C doesn't interpret chained comparisons mathematically. It evaluates:

C
(n > i) > 0

Since n = 4 and i ranges from 0 to 3, n > i is always true.

So you're actually calling the barrier for every replica, including R0 and R3.

That isn't breaking your experiment, because both proposer threads visit the replicas in the same order. But if you intended to synchronize between iterations, a clearer condition would be:

C
if (j < n - 1)
    pthread_barrier_wait(&replicas[i].barrier);

Also, you initialized R3's barrier but don't destroy it. You can clean that up afterward.

2. You synchronized the stages, but haven't guaranteed the split

Here's the more interesting detail.

Your code uses:

C
int voter_roll[] = {0, 2, 1, 3};

Both proposers use that same order.

Your barrier creates something like:

Step 1    R0 ───────────────── R0
                    ↓
                 BARRIER
                    ↓
Step 2    R2 ───────────────── R2
                    ↓
                 BARRIER
                    ↓
Step 3    R1 ───────────────── R1

That prevents either proposer from racing ahead through all the replicas before the other catches up.

But each stage still has a race over who reaches the replica's mutex first.

That's why you're now seeing split outcomes more frequently.

However, it's still possible for A to win all three stages and reach quorum.

Remember the earlier idea of giving each proposer a different order?

Proposal A: R0 → R1 → R2
Proposal B: R1 → R0 → R2

With a single shared two-thread barrier between stages, you get:

Stage	Proposal A	Proposal B
1	R0: YES	R1: YES
2	R1: NO	R0: NO
3	Both compete for R2

A wins R2

A: 2, B: 1

Neither commits

B wins R2

A: 1, B: 2

Neither commits

One important detail: with different visiting orders, the barrier needs to be the same barrier object for both proposer threads at each stage, not replicas[i].barrier, since A and B could otherwise wait on different barriers forever.

No synchronization: Honest replicas could accidentally approve contradictory proposals.

Per-replica mutexes: Honest replicas preserve their local voting invariant, even under competing requests.

Synchronized but competing proposals: All honest replicas can behave correctly, and the system can still fail to obtain a quorum.

And here's the key realization:

We can no longer fix the remaining problem simply by improving the local synchronization.

Your mutexes are doing their job. Your barrier is doing its job. The replicas aren't corrupting memory or accidentally changing votes.

The failure now exists in the agreement protocol itself.

That's a meaningful milestone because it brings us to the original Byzantine fault-tolerance question.

We've seen how to make individual participants behave correctly. Now we need to figure out how multiple independently correct participants can recover when they disagree.

} else if (b.approvals < QUORUM) {

Think about what this actually means.

Suppose:

A: 3 votes → COMMIT
B: 0 votes → REJECT

That's successful consensus!

A won the log position. B was correctly rejected.

But your code still sets:

C

because B didn't reach quorum.

In fact, since honest replicas cannot approve both conflicting proposals, at least one of A or B must fail to reach quorum.

So your condition effectively identifies every round as faulty, including successful ones.

That's a genuinely stalled voting round.

This is the really interesting part.

You added:

C

    printf("WAITING FOR BARRIER!\n");
    pthread_barrier_wait(&replicas[i].barrier);
}

The previous round failed. Maybe I can force the proposers to resynchronize so one gets enough votes this time.

But remember what our barrier actually guarantees:

Both proposers reach the same execution stage before either proceeds.

It does not guarantee that those proposers will agree.

R2 → B
R1 → A

The replicas still disagree.

And you've made an interesting architectural discovery:

Synchronizing when participants make decisions is not equivalent to coordinating which decision they should make.

That's the distinction we need for the next lesson.

4. The missing ingredient is coordination across rounds

Right now, every new round does this:

C
atomic_init(&replicas[i].vote, UNVOTED);

Then you start both proposers again.

So conceptually:

Round 0:

    ↓
    no quorum

Round 1:

    A and B compete again

    reset everything
    ↓
    A and B compete again

You've created repeated independent elections, not necessarily a consensus recovery protocol.

Nothing about the next round makes agreement more likely except differences in scheduling.

What real BFT-style protocols introduce is some method of coordinating the next proposal — commonly a designated leader for a view, together with rules for preserving previous voting and commitment evidence.

For our simplified experiment, imagine:

Round 0:
    A and B compete
    ↓
    no quorum

    a designated proposer suggests A
    ↓
    honest replicas evaluate A
    ↓
    quorum may form

That's already a much more purposeful recovery strategy than adding barriers.

Of course, now comes our original safety challenge: what if A actually committed in round 0, but another coordinator starts round 1 and tries to commit B?

We need some information about earlier rounds to survive, not just reset every replica's vote.

5. Two housekeeping details before you continue

Your pthread_mutex_init() and pthread_barrier_init() calls are inside the round loop. That means you're reinitializing synchronization objects that haven't all been destroyed. In particular, the mutexes are never destroyed, and R3's barrier isn't destroyed. Reinitializing an already initialized POSIX mutex is undefined behavior.

For this experiment, initialize your synchronization objects once before the round loop, then reset the voting state between rounds. Destroy the synchronization objects after the last round.

Also, you're printing a.fault and b.fault before you assign their new values, so those printed flags won't describe the failure you just detected.

That is exactly the flaw we want to expose.

This is why real BFT protocols use mechanisms such as new leaders, new voting rounds, and evidence of earlier votes or commitments to determine which proposals can safely be supported.

The goal isn't to make everyone follow the apparent majority. It's to make sufficient participants agree without contradicting an earlier committed decision.

I think that's an excellent progression, particularly because you're deliberately separating communication, state management, and concurrency control instead of trying to implement consensus all at once.

And there's something particularly valuable about doing this in C: you're going to encounter the distinction between network concurrency and thread concurrency firsthand.

For example, you can build a perfectly capable non-blocking server using poll() or epoll() with a single thread. Multiple connections can be active simultaneously, but their handlers don't necessarily execute simultaneously.

That's a fascinating distinction given everything we've been studying.

NETWORK CONCURRENCY
    multiple connections in progress
    non-blocking I/O
    event loop
           ↓
    possibly one execution thread
           ↓
    no simultaneous writes to local state

Compared with:

THREAD CONCURRENCY
    multiple execution contexts
           ↓
    potentially simultaneous state access
           ↓
    mutexes / atomics / synchronization

Non-blocking I/O doesn't inherently require multithreading. And that's worth exploring before introducing threads, because you may discover you can eliminate an entire class of local synchronization problems through architecture alone.

The next challenge then becomes especially interesting: even if each node processes its own messages sequentially, the three nodes still operate concurrently with respect to one another.

That's where our earlier lessons return at a higher level.

One suggestion as you build: keep the networking transport separate from the protocol logic. Ideally you'll eventually have something conceptually like:

C
void handle_message(struct Node *node, const struct Message *msg);

Your socket code receives and parses messages; your protocol code decides what they mean and how local state should change. That separation will make it dramatically easier to test consensus failures without debugging networking and voting logic simultaneously.

And one detail worth keeping in mind as you implement non-blocking sockets: TCP is a byte stream, not a message queue. A single recv() can return half a command, multiple commands, or anything in between. You'll want some kind of message framing, perhaps newline-delimited commands initially.

I particularly like your plan to see what breaks before applying the synchronization tools we've learned. Just remember that distributed disagreement doesn't necessarily mean a local data race. You may have three individually race-free C programs that still disagree about leadership.

That's the exact territory we want to explore next.

Take your time with this one. Once you have the nodes exchanging messages reliably, I think the really satisfying milestone will be watching them independently elect a leader with the Windows supervisor completely disconnected.

At that point, you won't just be simulating distributed consensus anymore. You'll have built the beginnings of an actual distributed system.

Ohhhhh, I see it! You're actually pretty close, but there are two important mistakes in how you've combined poll() with your existing socket handler.

The good news is that your general approach is sound. You've correctly started building an event loop to multiplex several TCP connections through one thread.

The problem isn't really poll() itself. It's when you're calling handle() and how you're managing the client file descriptors.

1. The main problem: You're handling the client before it's ready

Look at this section:

C
if (fds[i].fd == server_fd) {
    int client_fd = accept(server_fd, NULL, NULL);

    // ...

    make_nonblocking(client_fd);

    if (nfds < MAX_FDS) {
        fds[nfds].fd = client_fd;
        fds[nfds].events = POLLIN;
        nfds++;
    }

    handle(client_fd, &node);
    close(client_fd);
}

There's the problem!

You've told poll() to monitor the client for incoming data, but then you immediately call handle() and close the connection anyway.

Consider the actual sequence:

Windows                           Linux

connect()
    ──────────────────────────►  accept()

                                  make_nonblocking()
                                  add fd to poll()
                                  handle()
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                  recv()
                                  EAGAIN!
                                      │
                                  close(fd)

send("PING\n")
    ──────────────────────────►  Connection already closed

recv()
    Waits / gets no reply

The important detail is that an accepted TCP connection isn't necessarily ready to be read from.

Because you made it non-blocking, recv() can return -1 with errno == EAGAIN if the request hasn't arrived yet.

Your read_line() treats that as the end of the read:

C
ssize_t r = recv(fd, &c, 1, 0);
if (r <= 0) break;

So handle() returns without generating a response.

What we actually want
poll() detects listening socket
           ↓
accept new connection
           ↓
add client to poll() list
           ↓
RETURN TO EVENT LOOP
           ↓
poll() detects client has data
           ↓
read incoming data
           ↓
process command
           ↓
send response

Notice that accepting and reading are two separate events.

That's the central architectural difference from your previous blocking server.

2. You're also leaving closed sockets in your polling array

You've got:

C
fds[nfds].fd = client_fd;
nfds++;

Followed by:

C
close(client_fd);

But you haven't removed that descriptor from fds.

So the next poll() may encounter:

fds[0] = listening socket
fds[1] = CLOSED SOCKET
fds[2] = CLOSED SOCKET
fds[3] = CLOSED SOCKET
...

Eventually you reach MAX_FDS, and the server can't track any more clients.

Even worse, poll() can report POLLNVAL for those invalid descriptors, and your loop ignores everything except POLLIN.

This is why descriptor lifecycle management becomes important in event-driven networking.

4. How I'd fix it incrementally

Rather than rewriting your entire server, I'd do this in two passes.

Pass A — Get your existing protocol working under poll()

First, modify your accept branch to only accept and register the socket:

C
if (fds[i].fd == server_fd) {
    int client_fd = accept(server_fd, NULL, NULL);

    if (client_fd < 0) {
        if (errno != EAGAIN && errno != EWOULDBLOCK)
            perror("accept");
        continue;
    }

    if (nfds < MAX_FDS) {
        fds[nfds].fd = client_fd;
        fds[nfds].events = POLLIN;
        nfds++;
    } else {
        close(client_fd);
    }
}

Notice we removed:

C
handle(client_fd, &node);
close(client_fd);

Now the socket stays open until we receive data.

For your first test, you could leave the accepted client sockets in blocking mode and call your existing handle() once poll() reports POLLIN. Then close and remove the descriptor afterward.

That would get you a functioning intermediate implementation, although the handler would still block the event loop if a client sends only part of a request.

It's a debugging step, not the final non-blocking design.

Pass B — Make client I/O genuinely non-blocking

This requires one more architectural change.

Right now:

C
static void handle(int fd, struct Node *node)

does three different jobs:

read bytes
   ↓
interpret command
   ↓
write response

I'd separate the command-processing part into something like:

C
static void process_command(const char *line, struct Node *node,
                            char *out, size_t out_size);

Then the event loop can manage input independently:

POLLIN
   ↓
recv available bytes
   ↓
append to client's input buffer
   ↓
complete line received?
   ├── NO  → wait for more POLLIN events
   └── YES → process_command()
                  ↓
              queue response
                  ↓
               POLLOUT
                  ↓
              send pending bytes

This is necessary because TCP does not preserve message boundaries. A command such as LEADER 5 2\n could arrive in multiple recv() calls, and a non-blocking send() might transmit only part of a response.

A useful addition to your client state

C

struct Client {
    int fd;
    char input[MAX_LINE];
    size_t input_len;
    char output[MAX_LINE];
    size_t output_len;
    size_t output_sent;
};

Each connection remembers how much of its incoming message and outgoing response has been processed between polling events.

This is the point where the implementation becomes a genuine non-blocking server rather than a blocking handler surrounded by poll().

5. Two smaller things I noticed

You wrote:

C
int activity = poll(fds, nfds, port);

The third argument is a timeout in milliseconds, not a port number.

You probably intended:

C

Also, you parse a configurable port but bind to the constant:

C
.sin_port = htons(PORT)

Instead use:

C
.sin_port = htons(port)

Those aren't the primary cause of your failure when using port 5050, but they're worth correcting.

One particularly important idea to take away: O_NONBLOCK doesn't mean that reading and writing happen automatically or that operations wait their turn. It means the calls return instead of waiting when they cannot make progress.

poll() tells you when to attempt I/O. Your code is still responsible for maintaining the connection's state between those attempts.

That's the architectural adjustment you're very close to making. And it's going to be directly useful when your three Linux nodes start exchanging votes, heartbeats, and leader announcements independently.
